extracted.intended_audience: actors, improvisers, comedians, and theatre teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Keith Johnstone's principles and exercises for improvisational theatre — practical and philosophical guidance for creating spontaneous, collaborative, and truthful stage work (status, spontaneity, narrative, masks, rehearsal games).

rubrics_metrics.name: Status dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Every social interaction involves status shifts; actors can use status to create believable and compelling characters by conveying power and hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Become aware of how status is communicated through body language, tone, and movement. Use status games to explore shifts and relationships. Practical note from the text: "If you lower your status, people won't hit you, and if you raise it, they'll defer to you." Status is presented as a key to understanding all communication and a tool for crafting nuanced interactions on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting go of self-censorship and embracing quick, open responses to cultivate fresh, alive performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate openness and quick thinking through exercises that reduce fear of judgment and failure. Johnstone stresses that overthinking stifles creativity; techniques and games are used to train actors to respond spontaneously rather than pre-plan. Includes fostering an attitude of acceptance and exploration rather than safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes, and (accept and build)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique of accepting an offer and building on it — the 'magic of saying yes'— to keep scenes moving and generate surprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively accept what others provide and add to it. The post quotes: "Those who say ‘Yes’ are rewarded by the adventures they have. Those who say ‘No’ are rewarded by the safety they attain." Anti-pattern: saying 'No' shuts down possibilities and prioritizes safety over creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Building cohesive and entertaining scenes without pre-planning by trusting impulses and allowing stories to unfold organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize emotional truth and surprise over strictly logical or predetermined outcomes. Follow instincts and let narratives develop from the moment rather than forcing a logical plot. Johnstone encourages trusting impulse and valuing unexpected turns as part of storytelling in improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masks and trance
rubrics_metrics.description: Using masks as a tool to access primal emotions and physicality, enabling actors to shed personal identity and enter a trance-like state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masks help actors lose self-consciousness and inhabit other characters more fully, facilitating deeper emotional and physical expression. Use mask work deliberately to unlock different energy levels and embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal games and exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical exercises and games designed to break inhibitions, explore character relationships, and attack a text in rehearsal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnstone's book offers numerous games to get actors out of self-consciousness and overthinking. Use these exercises to experiment with status, spontaneity, physical choices, and ensemble dynamics as a route to authentic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness with commitment ('learn to play seriously')
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining a playful attitude with full commitment to choices on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take play seriously — be fully committed to playful impulses rather than half-heartedly joking. This mix of seriousness and play makes improvisation both joyful and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and releasing partner's imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvisor's role is to inspire and uplift scene partners, releasing their imagination rather than dominating the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize collaborative offers that enable others to build. Johnstone writes: "The improviser has to understand that his first skill lies in releasing his partner's imagination." Prioritize supporting choices that open possibilities for the ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-taking and embracing the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging actors to accept not knowing and take strange paths rather than seeking to be 'right'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward bold, unplanned choices; treat mistakes and uncertainty as sources of discovery. Quote: "People try to use what they know. They want to be ‘right.’ But I prefer to see people who don’t know what they’re doing and take strange paths." Trust in spontaneity grows with experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality / outside-in approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Working from physical action and embodiment to generate character and truthful behavior (an 'outside-in' method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book is noted as "great for physical actors who like to work from the outside-in." Use physical choices and movement to initiate character and emotional truth, emphasizing action over suppression: "In life, most of us are highly skilled at suppressing action. Action is a handicap. In the theatre, we do the opposite."

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble size and simplicity (smaller groups generate more ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller groups or simpler pairings encourage more creative possibilities in scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnstone observes: "The more people there are in a scene, the fewer ideas are generated. If only two people meet, there are limitless possibilities." Favor simplicity in casting and staging when you want generative invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv as exploration, not competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation should prioritize creativity, surprise, and openness rather than a win/lose competitive mindset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a non-competitive stance: the goal is shared discovery. The summary states: "Improvisation is not about winning; it’s about being creative and surprising and open." Avoid treating scenes as contests for jokes or dominance.
